name: Table grapes
why_now: California table grapes peak from late August through October, and September is when the good ones get cheap. This is the one thing in the basket that asks nothing of you — no technique, no recipe, no heat. Buy them, keep them cold, eat them.
how_to_choose: Green stems, not brown and brittle — that is the freshness tell, not the fruit
Grapes firmly attached; if they fall off the bunch, it is old
A dusty white bloom on the skin is a good sign, not dirt
Plump, with no shriveling where they meet the stem
Taste one if the market allows it. Sweetness does not increase after picking
buy_this_much: 1–2 lbs. One pound gets eaten; the second one becomes the drink.
price_note: The cheapest weeks of the year for grapes. Prices climb again by late fall when the domestic season ends and imports take over.

flavor_paths.name: Cold and plain
flavor_paths.description: Straight from the fridge. Do not overthink this one.

flavor_paths.name: Blended
flavor_paths.description: Into agua fresca with lime and a pinch of salt.

flavor_paths.name: Frozen
flavor_paths.description: On a tray in the freezer. Eaten like candy.

weekday_uses: Halved over Greek yogurt with honey
Frozen on a tray and eaten like candy
weekend_use: A bowl of cold grapes after the fish tacos.
storage: Unwashed, in their bag, in the coldest part of the fridge. Rinse only what you are about to eat; washed grapes turn soft in a day.
one_thing_to_learn: Grapes do not ripen after they are picked. Unlike the peaches and figs of the last two editions, a hard, sour grape stays a hard, sour grape on your counter forever, which is why the stem tells you more than the fruit does. Green, flexible stems mean the bunch came off the vine recently. Brown, dry, brittle stems mean weeks in a cooler, no matter how good the grapes still look.
